title: Strategy Contamination: Bot Is Executing Momentum Trades Disguised as Mean Reversion
analysis: Two executed BUY orders show signals that are the antithesis of mean reversion: NVDA on 2026-05-15 fired 'RSI>65 (strong momentum)', 'AboveMA20>1%', 'ADX>25 (trending)' — all trend/momentum signals, not mean reversion signals. AAPL on 2026-05-18 fired 'RSI>65 (strong momentum)', 'AboveMA20>1%', 'ADX>25 (trending)', 'A_GRADE setup'. Both were SUBMITTED. Meanwhile, the signal scoring system in CLAUDE.md only defines oversold/ranging signals (RSI<35, RSI<45, BelowBB, BelowMA20, ADX<25). The signals that actually triggered these live trades — RSI>65, AboveMA20>1%, ADX>25 — do not exist in the documented scoring system. This means an undocumented signal pathway is executing trades that violate Hard Rule #6 ('If ADX > 30, regime is TRENDING — do NOT take mean reversion signals'). The NVDA trade had ADX>25 confirmed trending, and was still submitted. The system is running a hybrid strategy without governance. Additionally, the MSFT SELL on 2026-05-18 at entry_price 419.81 with day_pl of -$306.95 shows the position was exited at a loss — the original MSFT entries rejected on 05-13 and 05-14 were at 404-408 range, suggesting MSFT ran up to ~420 and then reversed, meaning the bot held through a profitable window and exited on the downturn.
rationale: A mean reversion system buying overbought, above-MA20, trending stocks is not mean reversion — it is momentum trading without momentum risk controls (no trailing stops, no trend continuation rules, no sector rotation filters). These trades carry fundamentally different risk profiles than the documented strategy. When the regime shifts, momentum longs get caught in sharp reversals. The absence of these signals from the scoring documentation means they bypass all safety thresholds and cannot be reviewed, audited, or tuned. This is the single highest risk to capital.

insight.why_now: Two of the only three SUBMITTED trades in the 50-entry window are pure momentum entries that explicitly violate Hard Rule #6. With only ~4 actual executions visible in this log, a 50% contamination rate of executed trades is a critical finding. The Energy sector is +5.23% over 5 days while Technology is -0.48% — a rotation environment where momentum signals on tech names like NVDA and AAPL are particularly dangerous.
insight.purpose: Force all entry signals through the documented scoring system. Any signal not in the SIGNAL SCORING section must be prohibited from triggering a BUY. The trend filter in Rule #6 must function as a hard gate, not a soft suggestion.
insight.expected_effect: Eliminates strategy contamination. Prevents the system from silently switching strategies mid-session. Reduces the risk of holding momentum longs into reversals without appropriate exits. Makes the system auditable and consistent.
insight.risks: If the momentum trades were profitable, removing them reduces gross P&L opportunity. However, without a complete P&L record on the NVDA and AAPL exits, the actual contribution is unknown — and the structural risk of unaudited signal pathways outweighs potential upside.

current_rule: 6. TREND FILTER: If ADX > 30, regime is TRENDING — do NOT take mean reversion signals.
proposed_rule: 6. TREND FILTER: If ADX > 25, regime is TRENDING — do NOT take mean reversion signals. HARD BLOCK: Any signal combination containing RSI>65, AboveMA20>1%, or ADX>25 (trending) is PROHIBITED from triggering a BUY action regardless of score. Only signals listed in the SIGNAL SCORING section may contribute to entry decisions. Any trade with signals outside the SIGNAL SCORING section must be action=SKIP. Log violations as STRATEGY_CONTAMINATION.

title: Watchlist Concentration in Correlated Tech Names Is Starving Trade Throughput
analysis: Of 50 journal entries, 13 are rejections on META (4) and MSFT (9) alone — all blocked by the no-add-to-existing-position rule. The bot is generating valid signals (score 3+, R:R 2.58–3.7) repeatedly on the same 2 symbols it already holds, while finding zero qualifying signals on any other symbol. Open positions remain stuck at exactly 2 for the entire May 12–14 window and then 3 after the NVDA entry on May 15. The account sits at $98,237–$98,543 for three full trading days (May 12–14) generating no new entries despite 15+ scan cycles. META and MSFT are both large-cap tech (XLK sector), which is down -0.48% over 5 days — the weakest performing sector in the current macro context aside from Industrials (-2.06%). The system is over-indexed to a single sector that is currently underperforming, and the no-pyramid rule (correct in isolation) is creating a de facto trading freeze because the watchlist has no substitutes.
rationale: Mean reversion works best across a diverse set of range-bound instruments. Running a 2–3 symbol watchlist dominated by correlated tech megacaps means: (1) when both positions are open, the system effectively goes idle; (2) correlation between META and MSFT means both positions move together, doubling effective sector risk; (3) missed opportunity cost is visible — 13 rejected signals with R:R 2.58–3.7 over 3 days represents significant unrealized edge. Adding liquid, low-correlation mean reversion candidates (e.g., SPY, QQQ, GLD, XLE given its +5.23% 5d move suggesting range establishment after momentum, or defensive sector ETFs like XLV/XLP) would give the scanner alternatives when tech positions are saturated.

insight.why_now: The sector rotation data is decisive: Energy +5.23%, Tech -0.48%, Industrials -2.06%. The current watchlist is concentrated in the weakest-performing sector. Simultaneously, the system generated 13 blocked signals in 3 days — a direct, quantifiable throughput loss. The system is not underperforming because the strategy is wrong; it is underperforming because it has nowhere to deploy capital when its 2 tech positions are open.
insight.purpose: Expand the scannable universe to include 4–6 instruments across at least 3 uncorrelated sectors or asset classes. Prioritize instruments with documented mean reversion behavior: broad ETFs (SPY, QQQ), commodity ETFs (GLD, SLV), and sector ETFs from non-tech sectors currently showing range-bound behavior.
insight.expected_effect: Increases valid trade throughput from near-zero during multi-day hold periods. Reduces sector concentration risk. Allows capital to be deployed in mean reversion setups even when tech positions are fully loaded. With 2 open positions and a 5-position maximum, the system has 3 empty slots it cannot fill due to watchlist limitations.
insight.risks: Adding instruments without verifying their mean reversion suitability (via Bollinger Band squeeze history, ADX distribution, beta) could introduce directional stocks that fail mean reversion repeatedly. ETFs are lower-risk additions; individual momentum stocks should be vetted against ADX history before inclusion.

proposed_rule:
## WATCHLIST REQUIREMENTS
- Minimum 6 symbols spanning at least 3 uncorrelated sectors or asset classes.
- At least 2 slots must be broad or sector ETFs (e.g., SPY, QQQ, GLD, XLE, XLV, XLP) which have natural mean reversion properties.
- Individual stocks must have demonstrated range-bound behavior: median ADX < 25 over trailing 20 days before inclusion.
- No more than 2 symbols from the same GICS sector may be held simultaneously (correlation cap).
- Watchlist reviewed weekly against sector rotation data — rotate out symbols in strongly trending sectors (5d sector move > ±3%).

title: VIX 17.82 Transition Zone Requires Tightened Stop and Reduced Size vs Current Rules
analysis: Current VIX is 17.82 — above the low-vol threshold of 15 but below the elevated-fear threshold of 25. This is a transition zone. SPY is above its 20-day MA (738.65 vs 725.30, +1.84%), which is constructive for mean reversion on the long side. However, the sector rotation data shows a mixed regime: Energy +5.23% (commodity momentum), Industrials -2.06% (growth concern), Tech -0.48% (mild distribution). This is not a clean ranging environment — it has directional sector divergence characteristic of a rotation phase. The current hard stop at 0.5x ATR is appropriate for low-vol environments (VIX<15) but may be too tight for VIX 17.82, where intraday ATR expansion can stop out mean reversion entries before the reversion occurs. The MSFT position held May 13–18 (5 days) and exited at a loss on May 18 with day_pl -$306.95, suggesting the time stop (3 days) either was not enforced or the position was entered later than the journal shows — either way the stop framework did not protect capital on the largest visible loss. The daily loss limit of -4% ($3,929 on a ~$98,300 account) was not breached (max observed day_pl was -$354.92 on May 18, ~0.36% of account), so the macro risk framework is not the immediate problem.
rationale: At VIX 17.82 with sector rotation underway, mean reversion entries on individual tech stocks carry asymmetric downside: if rotation accelerates, oversold tech names can continue lower (sustained oversold), making the 0.5x ATR stop insufficient. A dynamic stop that widens slightly in higher-VIX environments (e.g., 0.75x ATR when VIX 16–22) reduces premature stop-outs while the position sizing rule (1.5% risk per trade) keeps dollar risk constant because quantity is adjusted to match the wider stop. This preserves the R:R gate at 1.5:1 minimum while making stops more regime-appropriate.

insight.why_now: VIX at 17.82 is elevated relative to the recent low-vol regime and sits in a zone historically associated with regime transitions. The MSFT loss and the pattern of positions being held beyond their 3-day time stop (MSFT opened ~May 13, still open May 18 = 5 days) suggests the current exit framework is not being enforced correctly at precisely the moment regime stress is present. Addressing this before VIX moves above 20 is preventive.
insight.purpose: Make stop distance a function of current VIX regime rather than a fixed ATR multiple. This ensures stops breathe with realized volatility, reducing noise-driven stop-outs in moderate-vol environments while maintaining hard dollar risk limits via position sizing.
insight.expected_effect: Fewer premature stop-outs on valid mean reversion setups in VIX 16–22 environments. The 3-day time stop enforcement needs a hard coded check — the MSFT trade running 5+ days is evidence the time stop is not functioning as a hard rule. Fixing time stop enforcement alone would have cut the MSFT loss earlier.
insight.risks: Wider stops with same % risk = smaller position sizes = smaller wins on successful trades. In a true low-vol environment, the wider stop may never be needed and just reduces position size unnecessarily. This is a second-order effect and acceptable given the capital protection mandate.

current_rule: 4. STOP LOSS: Always set stop loss at order time. Hard stop = 0.5x ATR below entry.
proposed_rule: 4. STOP LOSS: Always set stop loss at order time. Stop distance is VIX-regime adjusted: VIX < 16 → 0.5x ATR; VIX 16–22 → 0.75x ATR; VIX > 22 → 1.0x ATR. Position quantity is calculated AFTER stop distance is set so that dollar risk remains 1.5% of account regardless of ATR multiple. The 3-day time stop is a HARD EXIT — no discretion, no extensions. If a position is open at the start of day 4, it is closed at market open regardless of P&L. Log any time-stop exit as TIME_STOP_FORCED.
